title: 70 weeks and 2300 days
summary: Daniel's numerical prophecies - 70 weeks and 2300 days - read by the day-year principle. The 70 weeks point precisely to the Messiah (proof that Jesus is the Christ), and the 2300 days lead to the year 1844 and open up the theme of the cleansing of the heavenly sanctuary and the judgment.

sections.heading: The key to the numbers: a day for a year

items.comment: The vision ends with a riddle of a sentence: "unto two thousand three hundred evenings and mornings, then the sanctuary will be cleansed." The number cries out for a key.

questions.text: When a specific number appears in a prophecy, how can we sensibly test whether it means literal days or something longer?

items.comment: God Himself gives the conversion rate: "a day for a year I have appointed you." In the language of prophecy one day can symbolize one year.

questions.text: What does it give us that God Himself establishes the "day for a year" principle, rather than an interpreter inventing it?

items.comment: A second witness to the same principle: forty days of scouting = forty years of wandering - "a day for a year." Two texts confirm the rule.

questions.text: Why, for certainty in interpretation, is it important to have "two witnesses" to the same principle in Scripture?

items.label: the "day for a year" principle as the key to time prophecies
items.content: In symbolic prophecies (Dan 7-9; Rev 11-13) the time periods are read by the "day = year" principle, based on Num 14:34 and Ezek 4:6. The principle applies to symbolic prophecies, not to every number in the Bible. It is the foundation both for the 70 weeks (490 years) and for the 2300 days (2300 years). This is a hermeneutical assumption - it should be stated clearly and submitted to review, because the rest of the reckoning rests upon it.

items.label: Daniel's vision itself supplies the conversion rate
items.content: Importantly, Dan 8 not only calls for a key but also supplies one: since the number reaches to "the time of the end" (Dan 8:17,19), the evenings-mornings cannot be literal days but must mean years. It is worth citing the analysis of William Shea, who gathered 23 biblical arguments for the day-year principle and showed that Jewish interpreters were already applying it in the 2nd century BC. The principle, then, is not a late invention - it was known long before this application.

sections.heading: 70 weeks: a prophecy that points to the Messiah

items.comment: "Seventy weeks are decreed" for the people and the holy city - a time "cut off," with a concrete purpose: to put an end to sin and to "anoint the Most Holy." This is a foretelling of the Messiah's work.

questions.text: What does it say about God that He appoints for the future not only the course of empires, but also the exact time of His saving work?

items.label: "seventy sevens" and their threefold structure
items.content: The Hebrew phrase in Dan 9:24 literally reads "seventy sevens" (seventy times seven). By the day-year principle this gives 490 years. This period divides into three consecutive parts: 7 weeks (49 years), 62 weeks (434 years), and 1 final week (7 years). This internal structure matters, because it is precisely within the last "week" that the Messiah's work unfolds.

items.label: the "seventy weeks" and Jeremiah's "seventy years"
items.content: Daniel is praying over Jeremiah's prophecy of the "seventy years" of captivity (Dan 9:2; cf. Jer 25:11-12; 29:10) - and it is precisely then that he receives the prophecy of the "seventy weeks." Note that this proximity itself suggests the conversion: since "seventy years" is spoken of right alongside, the "seventy" in verse 24 should likewise be counted in years. The context thus reinforces reading the 70 weeks as 490 years.

items.comment: A starting point is given: "from the going out of the word to rebuild Jerusalem, unto the Anointed One." The prophecy is anchored in history.

questions.text: Why, for a prophecy's credibility, is it important that it has a clearly marked historical beginning?

items.label: the starting point of 457 BC and the two timelines
items.content: The standard view takes "the going out of the word to rebuild Jerusalem" (Dan 9:25) to be the decree from the seventh year of Artaxerxes, dated to 457 BC. From this point: 490 years (70 weeks) lead to the time of the ministry and death of the Messiah in the 1st century AD; 2300 years lead to the year 1844. The 70 weeks are "cut off" (Dan 9:24) from the longer period of 2300 days - hence the shared start. It is worth stressing that the decree of Cyrus and the decree of Darius concerned only the rebuilding of the temple, so they do not meet the condition of Dan 9:25; only the decree of Artaxerxes (Ezra 7:12-26) covers both the rebuilding and the restoration of Jerusalem's self-government. The date 457 BC itself rests on a reconstruction of Persian chronology and requires historical verification; it should be presented as an assumption, not as biblical text.

items.comment: "After the sixty-two weeks the Anointed One will be cut off." The prophecy foretells not only the Messiah's coming, but His death.

questions.text: What does it mean that the Messiah was to die "not for Himself" - for whom, then?

items.label: "will be cut off" as the violent death of the Messiah
items.content: The verb in Dan 9:26 (Hebrew root karat, "to cut off, to cut down") denotes a violent taking of life, not an ordinary departure. This is read plainly as the death of the Messiah: "in the middle of the week" His sacrifice puts an end to the sanctuary offerings, and the old ceremonial law finds its fulfillment. The very prophecy that foretells the coming of the Anointed One thus foretells the cross.

items.comment: In the middle of the last week the Messiah "puts an end to sacrifice" - His death makes the old offerings unnecessary. The cross is the center of this timeline.

questions.text: If Jesus' sacrifice "ends" the sanctuary offerings, what does that say about the sufficiency of His work?

items.comment: Jesus begins His ministry with the words "the time is fulfilled" - as if deliberately pointing to the appointed prophetic moment. The numbers in Daniel find a face.

questions.text: What changes in how we see Jesus once we grasp that His coming was foretold down to the time, not a matter of chance?

items.comment: Paul sums it up in a single phrase: "when the fullness of time had come, God sent His Son." The Messiah came not earlier and not later than was foretold.

questions.text: What does the precision with which the prophecy about the Messiah came true mean for your trust in the Bible?

sections.heading: 2300 days: the longer line and the cleansing of the sanctuary

items.comment: The angel confirms: "the vision is true," yet Daniel does not grasp the number 2300 and is left "without strength." Part of the vision called for a later explanation.

questions.text: Why does God reveal some prophecies gradually, rather than everything at once?

items.comment: Years later the angel returns to "give you understanding of the vision." The 70 weeks are "cut off" from the longer period of 2300 days - both lines have a shared start.

questions.text: What does it give us to link the 70 weeks (which clearly point to the Messiah) with the longer line of 2300 days?

items.label: "cut off" (Dan 9:24) and the shared starting point of the two lines
items.content: The verb used in Dan 9:24 (Hebrew root chatak, "to cut off, to set apart") suggests the marking out of a shorter period from a longer one. Note that the 70 weeks (490 years) are "cut off" from the 2300 days of Dan 8 - and since they are cut off from its beginning, both lines start at the same moment. That is why the date for the beginning of the 70 weeks also marks the beginning of the 2300 years. This is the key hinge that connects the prophecy of the Messiah with the prophecy of the sanctuary.

items.comment: Since it is "a day for a year," the 2300 days are 2300 years - from that same starting point they lead to the year 1844 and to the "cleansing of the sanctuary." This opens up, rather than closes, the theme of the judgment (study 25).

questions.text: If the 2300 years point to the beginning of a special work of God in heaven, what is worth learning about it next?

items.label: "evenings and mornings" as a number of years
items.content: The number 2300 is given in Dan 8:14 in an unusual way: "evenings-mornings." Note that the Hebrew phrase has no plural and no conjunction "and" - it is not 2300 separate evenings and mornings (1150 days), but 2300 full units, which by the day-year principle give 2300 years. From the shared point with the 70 weeks (457 BC) they lead to the year 1844.

items.label: the "cleansing/vindication" of the sanctuary (Dan 8:14)
items.content: The Hebrew verb in Dan 8:14 is rendered at times as "will be cleansed" or "will be restored to its rightful state / vindicated." This range of meaning matters: it concerns a restorative, judicial act, not merely a ritual washing. The form comes from the root tsadaq ("to be righteous"), hence the nuance of "vindication/restoration." The NT (Heb 8-9) links this with the heavenly ministry of Christ.

items.comment: The "sanctuary being cleansed" is no longer a building in Jerusalem - the NT points to the "true tabernacle" in heaven, where Christ ministers. This shifts our gaze from earth to heaven.

questions.text: What changes when we realize that Jesus carries out a real ministry in the heavenly sanctuary today?

items.comment: The letter to the Hebrews speaks plainly of the "cleansing" of the heavenly things and of Christ, who "intercedes for us." Here Daniel 8 and the Gospel meet.

questions.text: How does the stern language of "judgment/cleansing" connect with the good news of Jesus who intercedes?

items.label: the Day of Atonement as the key to the "cleansing of the sanctuary"
items.content: We read the "cleansing of the sanctuary" in the light of the Old Testament Day of Atonement (Hebrew yom kippur, "day of atonement/cleansing"; Lev 16; 23:26-32). It was an annual day of judgment whose chief emphasis was not dread, but the acquittal of the faithful who throughout the year had made use of the sacrifices. Its heavenly counterpart is the ministry of Christ - which is why the year 1844 introduces not the theme of fear, but the good news of a High Priest who stands on the side of His people.

application.text: Daniel's prophetic numbers are not a puzzle for the curious - they are an anchor for faith. The 70 weeks pointed to the time of the Messiah with surgical precision: this is a solid argument that Jesus really is the Christ. And the 2300 years lead to the year 1844 and turn our gaze toward heaven, where Jesus - our High Priest - carries out a real ministry on our behalf. A prophecy that came true so exactly in the past compels us to take seriously what it says about today.
application.challenge: This week, trace Dan 9:24-27 with a timeline in hand and notice how the starting point connects both lines. Then thank Jesus in your own words for coming "in the fullness of time" - exactly when He promised.
